messages.subject: Re: Different p-value with std.lv = TRUE vs. std.lv = FALSE
parts:
If your model is relatively straightforward, this means that the models are not the same.

When you  add std.lv = TRUE, you  are adding an additional constraint, you  need to relax a constraint somewhere else to keep the models the same. Do your  two models have the same degrees of freedom?

messages.author: 5d4f9e7f97c21008
messages.subject: Re: Different p-value with std.lv = TRUE vs. std.lv = FALSE
parts:
This issue has been around for a while. When using Wald tests, both parameter estimates and standard errors (and thus p-values) can change based on how you set the scale of a latent variable (with std.lv=TRUE you are fixing latent variances to 1 with std.lv=FALSE you are fixing the first factor loading to 1). Gonzalez & Griffin (2001) do a nice job talking about this issue: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11570231/

One additional note: model fit should be the same for both models so if you want a method of testing parameters that's not affected by how you set the scale nested model tests of parameters (likelihood ratio tests) avoid this issue.

Alex

messages.author: bc810b1d0900407f
messages.subject: Re: Different p-value with std.lv = TRUE vs. std.lv = FALSE
parts:
For the indirect effect in a mediation model, if you use bootstrapping, whethe you fix the loading to one or fix the factor variances to one should not matter, usually.

This can be demonstrated for the standardized indirect effect. It is a known characteristic of the standardized coefficients that they are the same whether we fix the first loadings or the factor variances to one (assuming single sample model and no equality constraints). So, for each bootstrap sample, the standardized indirect effect is the same whether we fix the loadings or the factor variances. The p-values in each bootstrap sample are irrelevant. Therefore, the bootstrap CI will also be the same.

-- Shu Fai

messages.subject: Re: Different p-value with std.lv = TRUE vs. std.lv = FALSE
parts:
This issue is interesting. Although it has been mentioned a long time ago (the paper by Gonzalez and Griffin is indeed a good one), somehow it is rarely discussed in the application of SEM, maybe except for the following recent paper:

Yuan, K.-H., Ling, L., & Zhang, Z. (2024). Scale-invariance, equivariance and dependency of structural equation models. Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal, 1–16. https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2024.2353168

As suggested, the likelihood ratio test (LRT, a.k.a. chi-square difference test) is invariant to the choice of the method to set the scales of the factors: fixing the factor variance to one or fixing a loading to one. Practically, this is what we may "really" want: What is the change in fit, tested by the LRT, if we fix a parameter to zero.

One practical advantage of the usual Wald p-values, reported in lavaan and many other SEM programs by default, over the LRT, is computational. To use LRT, we need to fit one more model for each parameter. For the Wald p-value, all the p-values can be computed without fitting another model.

Mark Lai and I developed a package, semlrtp, to see whether we can make the computation of the LRT p-values more accessible. This is an illustration:

https://sfcheung.github.io/semlrtp/articles/semlrtp.html

What it does is very simple (in principle): For each selected parameter, e.g., a factor correlation, fit a model with this parameter fixed to zero, do the LRT to compare this model with the original model, and report the p-value.

This is a demo. First, we fit a 3-factor CFA model:

library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-19
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
library(semlrtp)

# Use fewer cases to demonstrate the functions
dat <- data_sem16[1:100, ]

mod <-
"
f1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4
f2 =~ x5 + x6 + x7 + x8
f3 =~ x9 + x10 + x11 +x12
"

We fit two models, one with the first loadings fixed to one, the other with the factor variances fixed to one

# Fix the first loadings to 1
fit_v1 <- sem(mod,
              dat)
# Fix the factor variances to 1
fit_v2 <- sem(mod,
              dat,
              std.lv = TRUE)

Compare the model fit. The two models are identical in fit, as expected.

The function lrtp() from the semlrtp package is then used to compute the LRT p-values for free parameters. By default, it only computes the LRT p-values for regression coefficients and covariances, to save computational time. I added op = c("=~", "~~") to compute LRT p-values for factor loadings too:

# Compute the LRT p-values
fit_v1_lrtp <- lrtp(fit_v1,
                 op = c("=~", "~~"))
fit_v2_lrtp <- lrtp(fit_v2,
                 op = c("=~", "~~"))

We then compare the LRT p-values for the free parameters in the two models. As expected, the LRT p-values are identical. They are the same whether we fixed the first loadings to one or fixed the factor variances to one:

Not demonstrated above, but the LRT p-values are also invariant to the choice of the reference indicators, the items with loadings fixed to one.

Note that, behind the scenes, the function just does what we ourselves can do manually:

- For the p parameters, we manually fit p more models,
- do p chi-square difference tests, and
- get the p-values.

Its goal is to do this as automatically as possible.

Being automatic comes at a cost. In trying the package, we found there are cases in which the computation may fail, e.g., Heywood cases may occur. We are working on this. There are also cases in which it does not make sense to fix a parameter to zero (though, for these parameters, the p-values may not be meaningful anyway).

In any case, for such "difficult parameters," we can find the LRT p-values manually and try to tweak the settings in fitting the model.

We are still exploring ways to improve the function. Comments and suggestions are welcome.

On mediation, if bootstrapping is used, then whether we fix the loadings to one or fix the factor variances to one should not matter. There should be some references on this, but I can't recall any. For the standardized indirect effects, this can be easily proved for a single sample model. For each bootstrap sample, whether we fix the loadings or fix the factor variances, the standardized parameters are the same. This is a known feature of the standardized solution. Therefore, the bootstrap estimates of the standardized indirect effect must also be the same. So, the bootstrap CIs are the same whether we fix the loadings or fix the factor variances.

-- Shu Fai

This issue is an interesting one, raised a long time ago, but rarely discussed in the application of SEM. This is another related paper:

Yuan, K.-H., Ling, L., & Zhang, Z. (2024). Scale-invariance, equivariance and dependency of structural equation models. Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal. https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2024.2353168

The p-values reported by many SEM programs are, by default, the Wald p-values, which are not invariant to the parameterization of the model. The likelihood ratio test (LRT, a.k.a., chi-square difference test) p-value may be what we usually "really" want: If we fix a parameter to zero, is the model fit significantly different from the original model? This test yields the same p-value whether we fix a factor loading to one or fix the factor variances to one.

One obvious drawback of the LRT p-values is the computational cost. For Wald p-values, we don't have to fit another model. For LRT p-values, we need to fit one more model for each parameter.

To try making LRT p-values more accessible and address the issue with the Wald p-value, Mark Lai and I developed a package, semlrtp. This is a demonstration of how to use it:

https://sfcheung.github.io/semlrtp/articles/semlrtp.html

What it does is basically this:

For each free parameter with the LRT p-value requested:
- Fit a model with this parameter fixed to zero.
- Do the LRT.
- Report the p-value.

This is demonstration using a 3-factor CFA model:

library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-19
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
library(semlrtp)

# Use fewer cases to demonstrate the functions
dat <- data_sem16[1:100, ]

mod <-
"
f1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4
f2 =~ x5 + x6 + x7 + x8
f3 =~ x9 + x10 + x11 +x12
"
Two models are fitted, one with the first loadings fixed to one, the other with the factor variances fixed to one:

# Fix the first loadings to 1
fit_v1 <- sem(mod,
              dat)
# Fix the factor variances to 1
fit_v2 <- sem(mod,
              dat,
              std.lv = TRUE)
As expected, these two models have identical goodness of fit:

# Compare model fit
fit_v1
#> lavaan 0.6-19 ended normally after 52 iterations
#>

#>
#>   Number of observations                           100
#>
#> Model Test User Model:
#>
#>   Test statistic                                63.442
#>   Degrees of freedom                                51
#>   P-value (Chi-square)                           0.113
fit_v2
#> lavaan 0.6-19 ended normally after 22 iterations
#>
#>   Estimator                                         ML
#>   Optimization method                           NLMINB
#>   Number of model parameters                        27
#>
#>   Number of observations                           100
#>
#> Model Test User Model:
#>
#>   Test statistic                                63.442
#>   Degrees of freedom                                51
#>   P-value (Chi-square)                           0.113
However, the p-values of free parameters can be different, sometimes non-negligibly, unless they are very small (e.g., p < .001).

The function lrtp() can be used to compute the LRT p-values. By default, it only computes LRT p-values for regression coefficients ("~") and covariances ("~~", error variances and variances are excluded), to save computational cost. Therefore, I used op = c("=~", "~~" ) to compute LRT p-values for factor loadings too:

# Compute the LRT p-values
fit_v1_lrtp <- lrtp(fit_v1,
                 op = c("=~", "~~"))
fit_v2_lrtp <- lrtp(fit_v2,
                 op = c("=~", "~~"))
As shown below, the LRT p-values are the same in both models for parameters that are free in both models:

fit_v2_lrtp

#>     x4                0.323    0.150    4.450    0.035

#>   f3 =~
#>     x9                0.929    0.137   39.408    0.000

#> Covariances:
#>                    Estimate  Std.Err    Chisq     LRTp
#>   f1 ~~
#>     f2                0.470    0.184    5.563    0.018
#>     f3                0.593    0.147   12.189    0.000
#>   f2 ~~
#>     f3                0.531    0.141   10.540    0.001

Not demonstrated above, the LRT p-values are also invariant to the choices of the items with their loadings fixed to one.

Being automatic comes at a cost. In trying the packages, we found cases in which the computation failed, because the model with a parameter fixed to zero failed to converge or had Heywood cases. We are working on this.

In any case, the function just does what we can do manually. Therefore, for these "difficult parameters," if we want to have the LRT p-values, we can fit the model manually and tweak some settings, such as the bounds.

There are cases in which the LRT p-value cannot be computed because the model with a parameter fixed to zero does not make sense and cannot be fitted. Nevertheless, for these parameters, perhaps the null hypothesis itself may not be meaningful anyway.

We are still exploring ways to improve this package. Comments and suggestions are welcome.

-- Shu Fai
On Friday, July 18, 2025 at 2:57:41 AM UTC+8 alexander...@gmail.com wrote:

This issue has been around for a while. When using Wald tests, both parameter estimates and standard errors (and thus p-values) can change based on how you set the scale of a latent variable (with std.lv=TRUE you are fixing latent variances to 1 with std.lv=FALSE you are fixing the first factor loading to 1). Gonzalez & Griffin (2001) do a nice job talking about this issue: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11570231/

One additional note: model fit should be the same for both models so if you want a method of testing parameters that's not affected by how you set the scale nested model tests of parameters (likelihood ratio tests) avoid this issue.

Alex

The function lrtp() can be used to compute the LRT p-values. By default, it only computes LRT p-values for regression coefficients ("~") and covariances ("~~", error variances and variances are excluded), to save computational cost. Therefore, I used op = c("=~", "~~" ) to compute LRT p-values for factor loadings too:

# Compute the LRT p-values
fit_v1_lrtp <- lrtp(fit_v1,
                 op = c("=~", "~~"))
fit_v2_lrtp <- lrtp(fit_v2,
                 op = c("=~", "~~"))

Not demonstrated above, the LRT p-values are also invariant to the choices of the items with their loadings fixed to one.

Being automatic comes at a cost. In trying the packages, we found cases in which the computation failed, because the model with a parameter fixed to zero failed to converge or had Heywood cases. We are working on this.

In any case, the function just does what we can do manually. Therefore, for these "difficult parameters," if we want to have the LRT p-values, we can fit the model manually and tweak some settings, such as the bounds.

There are cases in which the LRT p-value cannot be computed because the model with a parameter fixed to zero does not make sense and cannot be fitted. Nevertheless, for these parameters, perhaps the null hypothesis itself may not be meaningful anyway.

We are still exploring ways to improve this package. Comments and suggestions are welcome.

On Friday, July 18, 2025 at 2:57:41 AM UTC+8 alexander...@gmail.com wrote:

This issue has been around for a while. When using Wald tests, both parameter estimates and standard errors (and thus p-values) can change based on how you set the scale of a latent variable (with std.lv=TRUE you are fixing latent variances to 1 with std.lv=FALSE you are fixing the first factor loading to 1). Gonzalez & Griffin (2001) do a nice job talking about this issue: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11570231/

One additional note: model fit should be the same for both models so if you want a method of testing parameters that's not affected by how you set the scale nested model tests of parameters (likelihood ratio tests) avoid this issue.

Alex
